summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed summary judgment for a caseworker and a state trooper, holding that removal of all five children was supported by an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse and an imminent threat of abuse, and that a post-deprivation hearing three business days after the removal satisfied procedural due process.
key_cases.relevance: The decision states both the substantive threshold for an emergency removal decision and the timing requirement for the hearing that must follow.
key_cases.quote: no substantive due process violation is stated if there existed a reasonable suspicion that abuse had occurred or that a threat of abuse was imminent at the time of removal

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: In a case arising from a New Hampshire DCYS investigation and ex parte removal, the court affirmed dismissal of the 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claims against a court-appointed psychologist and her supervisor because the complaint stated no violation of any federal constitutional right, and affirmed dismissal of the state law claims as barred by the reporter immunity of RSA 169-C:31.
key_cases.relevance: The decision defines the federal constitutional exposure of the officials whose work supports an emergency removal order in New Hampshire.
key_cases.quote: the relationship between parent and child may be investigated and terminated by the state provided constitutionally adequate procedures are followed

key_cases.case_name: Hatch v. Department for Children, Youth & Their Families (State of Rhode Island)
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court held that the Constitution permits a caseworker to take a child into temporary custody without a prior hearing when the caseworker has a reasonable suspicion that abuse has occurred or that a threat of abuse is imminent, and affirmed the denial of leave to amend because the caseworker had such a suspicion and was entitled to qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: The court expressly rejected a probable cause or imminent-serious-bodily-injury requirement, fixing reasonable suspicion as the constitutional floor for the emergency removal decision.
key_cases.quote: Because the welfare of the child is paramount, an objectively reasonable suspicion of abuse justifies protective measures.
